drills.q: What are the four parts of an x86-64 memory operand?
options: Base register, index register, scale, and displacement
Segment, page, offset, and permission
Base, limit, index, and stride
Register, immediate, shift, and extend
drills.why: The processor adds them as part of the load, so one instruction covers what the source spells as a multiply, an add and a dereference.

drills.q: Which scale factors does the encoding allow?
options: Any power of two up to 128
Any value from 1 to 15
Only 1 and 8
drills.why: They are the sizes that matter for arrays of bytes, shorts, ints and pointers. Anything else costs an extra instruction, which is why struct sizes get rounded up in code that indexes them hard.

options: Computes an address and writes it to a register, without any memory access
Loads a value from an address into a register
Loads the address of the next instruction
Computes an address and prefetches the cache line
drills.why: It is the closest thing x86-64 has to a three-operand arithmetic instruction: it adds, scales, adds a constant, and writes somewhere that is not either input.

drills.q: Why do compilers use lea for arithmetic that has nothing to do with addresses?
options: It multiplies by 3, 5 or 9 in one instruction and leaves the flags alone
It is shorter to encode than add
It executes on a port add cannot use
It avoids a dependency on the destination register
drills.why: An instruction that does arithmetic without disturbing a comparison in progress is more useful than one that does not, and that is the same design pressure the flags create everywhere else.

options: A subtraction whose result is discarded, keeping only the flags
A dedicated comparison unit separate from the adder
An exclusive or followed by a zero test
A subtraction that saturates rather than wrapping
drills.why: test is the same trick with a bitwise and, which is why test rax, rax is how every compiler asks whether a value is zero.

drills.q: After one cmp, how does the processor know whether you meant signed or unsigned?
options: It does not; the jump you write afterwards picks the interpretation
From the register widths involved
From a mode bit set by the operating system
From whether the operands were loaded with sign extension
drills.why: It performs one subtraction and sets every flag. jb reads carry and asks the unsigned question; jl compares sign against overflow and asks the signed one.

drills.q: Comparing 0xFF against 0x01 in a byte. Which is larger?
options: Both answers are correct: 0xFF is above as unsigned and below as signed
0xFF, because the comparison is unsigned by default
0x01, because the top bit makes 0xFF negative
It is undefined without a signedness annotation
drills.why: As unsigned that is 255 against 1; as signed it is -1 against 1. The bits are identical and only the jump records which you wanted.

drills.q: What does the carry flag mean after an addition?
options: The unsigned result did not fit, and this is the bit that did not
The signed result had the wrong sign
The result was zero
A borrow occurred from a lower word
drills.why: It is why multi-word addition works: add the low words, then add the high words plus the carry.

drills.q: What does the overflow flag mean after an addition?
options: Two operands of one sign produced a result of the other, so the signed answer is wrong
The result exceeded the register width
The result required a carry out of the top bit
The operation saturated
drills.why: Add 0x7F and 0x01 in a byte and you get 0x80, which as signed is -128. Two positives cannot produce a negative, so the flag says the answer is wrong.

drills.q: What is the advantage of a conditional move over a branch?
options: Nothing to predict, and it takes the same time whichever way the condition goes
It is always faster
It uses fewer registers
It can be executed speculatively where a branch cannot
drills.why: That makes it a win for unpredictable conditions and a loss for predictable ones, since a correctly predicted branch is nearly free while a conditional move always waits for its input.

drills.q: Why is cryptographic code written with conditional moves?
options: Constant time either way means the timing does not leak which branch was taken
They cannot be reordered by the processor
They are immune to speculative execution attacks
They avoid touching the flags
drills.why: It is the same property that makes them useful for unpredictable branches, used for a different reason, and Part XV depends on it.

drills.q: What happens if an add sits between a cmp and the branch that reads it?
options: The branch tests the addition's flags, silently, because nothing in the syntax connects them
The assembler warns about a flag dependency
The processor preserves the older flags for the branch
Nothing, since add writes only the carry flag
drills.why: The flags are one register written by almost every arithmetic instruction, so the distance between setting them and using them is not free to choose.

drills.q: Why do compilers emit add 1 rather than inc?
options: inc updates every flag except carry, and merging the old carry has cost a stall
inc is longer to encode
inc cannot address memory
inc is deprecated in 64-bit mode
drills.why: A hand-written inc in a hot loop has been a measurable regression more than once, for exactly this reason.

drills.q: What does mov rax, [rip + offset] buy you?
options: The block can be loaded anywhere, since nothing in the encoding names an absolute address
Faster loads, since the address needs no register
Access to memory above the four gigabyte boundary
Automatic bounds checking against the code segment
drills.why: It is what makes position-independent executables possible and address space layout randomisation able to move things.

drills.q: How did position independence work on 32-bit x86?
options: It cost a register and a helper call per access, because there was no such addressing mode
It was not supported at all
The loader rewrote every absolute address at load time
A segment register held the base and was added automatically
drills.why: Adding one addressing mode removed a whole category of overhead, which is why position independence is the default everywhere now.
